newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-BankAmerica sees Mexico loan competition.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-BankAmerica sees Mexico loan competition.

text.p: Mexico's competitive commercial paper and loan market has driven spreads sharply lower and allowed borrowers to increase the size and extend maturities of their debt issues, Lorenzo Gonzalez Bosco, vice president of BankAmerica Corp's Bank of America, said.

Bank of America arranged seven U.S. commercial paper issues in Mexico in 1996 worth a total of $2.285 billion. The companies were some of Mexico's biggest, including Petroleos Mexicanos, Cemex SA, Grupo Financiero Bancomer SA de CV and development bank Nacional Financiera, Nafin.
That short-term paper and loan market has changed as Mexico's economy has recovered.

"The market has changed significantly. As Mexico has recovered from the crisis, we have seen that the market is moving from the very short tenors (or maturities) to medium-term financing," Gonzalez, also business director, told Reuters in an interview.

"In early 1995 most of the loans made to Mexican companies just after the crisis were for no more than 30, 60 or 90 days. Now we are seeing a big appetite from the foreign banks to arrange credits up to five years," he said.
As well, the U.S. commercial paper market is very deep and efficient, particularly for those Mexican companies that can obtain an investment-grade rating.

"We have seen companies that already have programs who are looking for longer tenors and larger amounts, and we also see a group of companies who have large needs for working capital financing, making it feasible for them to implement a U.S. commercial paper program," Gonzalez said, adding that unless they are looking for more than $100 million, the programs do not make sense.
"All the issuers are looking for longer tenors. The market has been very receptive to five-year transactions. I don't think the banking community will go further than that," he said.
Beyond five years, bonds become more attractive.
For Mexican companies in good financial shape, there are a wide range of borrowing opportunities, ranging from commercial paper, to medium-term Euronotes, to bonds, or to the equity markets.
"The equity market is open as well, although it is less interesting at current prices," he said.
"By the end of the year it will be very attractive for them (to place equity issues)."
With all the options available and tight competition, spreads have fallen as supply outstrips demand.

"When we were making loans over six or seven percent over LIBOR for short-term periods in 1995, in 1997 our loans for the same tenor are no more than one percent over LIBOR. This shows you how dramatically the spreads have dropped," he said.
"Eventually we will reach a limit. I don't think that they will go down significantly; however, there is still some room to go down.
"Basically this is a result of a very few good companies that can access international credit versus a large number of foreign banks that are aggressively seeking business in Mexico," he said.

Many never left Mexico after the peso crash, and more banks started coming in as the economy began to recover, leading some analysts to say that the country is "overbanked" by investment and commercial bankers.
There are also a limited number of Mexican companies in good enough financial condition to access international financial market, analysts said.
Bank of America is, however, working to build up its peso loan portfolio.
Until 1995 the bank was limited to dollar lending in Mexico, but after opening Bank of America Mexico, a corporate banking subsidiary, it began to develop the local market.
"As part of that, we are actively building up a peso portfolio," Gonzalez said. "We are lending to companies in sound financial condition, from medium-sized to large corporates."
